mcq.q: On 1 March, Raju agrees to supply 100 bags of rice to Shyam on 1 June. On 10 April Raju writes that he will not supply. Under Section 39, Shyam:
options: Must wait till 1 June before taking any action
Can only claim the price of rice on 10 April
Has no remedy until Raju actually fails to deliver
May treat the contract as ended at once and sue for damages, or may wait till 1 June
mcq.explain: A refusal before the due date is anticipatory breach. Section 39 allows the promisee to treat the contract as over immediately and sue, unless he has signified acquiescence in its continuance. He may instead choose to keep the contract alive till the due date, but then he takes the risk of later events.
mcq.fast: Refusal BEFORE due date = anticipatory breach: two choices — rescind now or wait.

mcq.q: Section 73 does NOT allow compensation for:
options: Loss flowing naturally from the breach in the ordinary course
Remote and indirect loss caused by the breach
Losses that both parties knew, when they made the contract, would likely result
Reasonable expenses of finding a substitute
mcq.explain: Section 73 compensates two kinds of loss: loss that flows naturally from the breach in the ordinary course, and loss both parties foresaw as likely when they contracted. Losses that are remote or indirect are expressly excluded — the principle of Hadley v. Baxendale.
mcq.topic: Suit for damages — Section 73 and Hadley v. Baxendale
mcq.fast: Natural or foreseen loss = yes; remote and indirect loss = no.

mcq.q: A mill's broken shaft is handed to a carrier for repair; the carrier is not told that the mill is idle without it. Delivery is delayed. The mill-owner's claim for lost profits will:
options: Fail — the loss was not foreseen by the carrier and is too remote (Hadley v. Baxendale)
Succeed because delay is always a breach
mcq.explain: Under Section 73 and the rule in Hadley v. Baxendale, damages cover losses arising naturally or those in the contemplation of both parties at the time of contract. The carrier did not know that the mill would stop without the shaft, so lost profits were special damage it never contemplated and are too remote.
mcq.topic: Suit for damages — Section 73 and Hadley v. Baxendale
mcq.fast: Special loss is recoverable only if the special facts were told at the time of contract.

mcq.q: A contract names ₹2,00,000 as the sum payable on breach. On breach, the court assesses reasonable compensation at ₹80,000. Under Section 74 the aggrieved party gets:
options: Nothing, since a sum named in the contract is a penalty and is void
mcq.explain: When the contract itself names a figure for breach, Section 74 gives the injured party reasonable compensation up to that figure, and proof of actual loss is not essential. Indian law does not automatically enforce the full stipulated sum; the court fixes a reasonable figure within the ceiling.
mcq.fast: Section 74: the named sum is a CEILING; the court gives "reasonable compensation".

mcq.q: Damages awarded to punish the defaulting party, as in wrongful dishonour of a customer's cheque by a bank despite sufficient funds, are called:
mcq.explain: Exemplary or vindictive damages go beyond compensation to punish the defendant. In contract law they are given rarely — for breach of a promise to marry, and for a banker's wrongful dishonour of a cheque when the customer had enough funds, since it injures the customer's reputation. Nominal damages only recognise a right that was violated.

mcq.q: A builder abandons work halfway because the owner wrongfully stops him. The builder can recover the value of work done through:
mcq.explain: Quantum meruit means "as much as earned". When a contract is discharged by the other party's breach after partial performance, the party who performed can claim reasonable remuneration for the work done. Specific performance and injunction are orders to do or not do something, and exemplary damages are punitive.
mcq.topic: Other remedies — rescission, quantum meruit, specific performance, injunction
mcq.fast: Paid for work already done = quantum meruit.

mcq.q: A singer agrees to sing only at Theatre A for one season and not elsewhere, then agrees to sing at Theatre B. Theatre A can obtain:
options: An injunction restraining her from singing at Theatre B
Specific performance forcing her to sing at Theatre A
mcq.explain: Courts do not compel performance of contracts for personal service, so specific performance is not available. But a negative stipulation — not to sing elsewhere — can be enforced by injunction (Lumley v. Wagner). Theatre A may also claim damages. Mandamus is a writ against public authorities, not private parties.
mcq.topic: Other remedies — rescission, quantum meruit, specific performance, injunction
mcq.fast: Negative promise ("not elsewhere") -> injunction. Personal service is never specifically enforced.
